It is quite common these days that the young are much influenced by peer pressure. It is my belief that the positive effects of this phenomenon could certainly offset its disadvantages. 

There are several drawbacks to peer pressure. A common reason is that young people’s mentality is negatively affected, which can lead to worry or depression. In fact, working or studying with better students can make young people uncomfortable. For example, when I study in a class with a lot of classmates who learn much better than me, I feel very pressured and ashamed. Another negative aspect can be that the youth often feel uncomfortable with their appearance. This means that if peers just pay attention too much attention to appearance and make judgments, young people can feel uneasy and try to be as  fashionable as possible, which can be very costly.

However, in spite of these negative effects, peer pressure can bring about important benefits. One obvious advantage is that young people have opportunities and environments to develop themselves better. In fact, if young people are surrounded by good people, they can learn from them such as trying anything new or discovering new ideas to help them overcome some difficult problems. For example, my colleagues in my brother’s company work productively and solve problems quickly; therefore, my brother day by day works more effectively and productively, and he has just been promoted to manager. 

In conclusion, it’s common that young people are often influenced in their behaviours and situations by peers. While this can make them sometimes stressed, there can be a lot of benefits in helping young people to have  motivation to grow and succeed.

prompt.text: Many university graduates cannot find a job in their chosen profession. What factors may have caused this situation and what, in your opinion, should be done about it?

essay.text:
When young people are choosing what subject to study at university, most of them hope they will find a great job upon graduation. In reality many fresh graduates fail to find work in their field and some are even forced to take up a below graduate level job. In my opinion, the root of this problem lies in the outdated higher education system that should be modernized.
Traditional university education does not prepare students for their first job for a number of reasons. One of them is that many programmes are too theoretical. It means that highly educated graduates lack simple skills required for employment, for example, the knowledge of IT software. Employers, therefore, prefer candidates with hands-on experience. Another reason is that universities offer too many courses in popular fields, such as business and law, and do not recruit enough students for engineering and science programmes. As a result, the UK labour market has an oversupply of law graduates and a deficit of engineers. 
A reform of higher education could alleviate many of the problems but would require joint efforts from universities and the government. If universities worked closer with employers, they could teach students practical skills that companies look for. Meanwhile, the government could develop guidelines on how many students universities should recruit in each subject in accordance with the market demand.
In conclusion, a likely reason why many graduates cannot find a job in their field is because university education might not have provided them with the right skill set or an in-demand profession. I think that universities and the government could improve the situation by updating the content of the programmes and limiting the number of students in each subject in line with the market demand.

Recently along with those who choose to continue further study in universities after high school graduation, there are a considerable number of  young learners deciding to take a gap year for travelling or working before going straight to university. In this essay, I will clarify both the merits and demerits of this movement for school leavers’ education.

To begin with, the trend towards delaying further education is beneficial to high school graduates with their later studies. In particular, school leavers receive opportunities to explore their potential and life goals before attending any higher educational institutions. By doing part-time jobs and travelling to different regions domestically or abroad, the young can relax their mind, identify their interests, and find their inspirations for further study. This betters their decision-making in terms of choosing the right majors and future careers. If the young can not study their suitable academic field in college, they are likely to lose motivation and interest towards their education. Consequently, it prevents them from achieving better academic results. Moreover, gap years for individuals facilitate the graduates to learn practical skills which are necessary to their major. Many students find it incomprehensible knowledge taught at universities or colleges, which may affect their academic results. For this reason, if the young are exposed to real working environments where they can learn  several skills related to their desired educational field, they will find the knowledge gained in universities relevant and informative to their later career path. As a result, they can attain higher academic achievements.

However, this trend also implicit several drawbacks to young people’s academic learning. One of the disadvantages is break years are counter-productive for those who do not possess  great concentration, firm determination, and self-discipline as they can not make great use of the break and waste it for fruitless interests such as playing games or sleeping in, … A further point that can be taken into consideration is that some young learners can be so tempted by earning money or having a break that they discontinue their education. 

In conclusion, although working or travelling before going to university might be ideal for young people thanks to its numerous benefits, they shouldn’t overlook its hidden disadvantages.

essay.text:
There is fierce competition between nations to host major international sports events like the World Cup or Olympics as it is a unique opportunity to boost the national reputation of the host nation. The efforts made to cater to these tourists will remain long after they have gone. The cost of renovating a hotel might pay for itself during the event and then begin turning a large profit in later years. Nations will be forced to invest in new sports facilities like swimming pools and stadiums as well as make renovations to pre-existing infrastructure like roads and airports. For example, China used the Beijing Olympics as an opportunity to modernise old buildings and roads. 
On the other hand, these competitions use up tremendous resources from the host nation for a temporary competition. To ensure the success of these prestigious events, governments must waste a large percentage of the nation budget in the years leading up to the competition, oftentimes in the billions of dollars. The newly constructed facilities usually fall into disuse after each tournament. A salient example of this is Brazil as many of the swimming pools and sports facilities that were used in the 2014 Olympics are currently abandoned and becoming decrepit. Meanwhile, there are other pressing issues that have been festering including the need for new schools for underprivileged students and quality healthcare for the elderly population. If the government had prioritised these issues the country would be in a better position and its citizens would have a higher standard of living. 
To summarize, due to the exorbitant costs, I am of the belief that the government should not allocate such a large percentage of its financial resources to hosting global events with negligible long-term impact. Instead these events should be hosted in the same countries year after year so that the new infrastructure pays for itself over time.

In conclusion, watching TV in excess can be detrimental for children, but I believe that it could be educational if seen if watched for a short amount of time under parental supervision.

This essay will delve into the positive and negative aspects of the phenomenon and outline which factors matter the most.

The prominent advantage provided by social media platforms is instant gratification. At the click of a button, the world is on your doorstep. Being a social animal, the feeling of connectedness is the innate desire for all human beings. Being able to fulfil this need is the crucial driving factor for the success of all Social media platforms. Conversely, the attractiveness of Social media is leading us to a  significant chasm in everyday human interactions that is critical for the human race as a whole. People are content with scrolling through life updates of a friend/ family member and getting influenced by fake news published on such websites. The conventional concept of meeting in person and celebrating together is dying its slow death. People have stopped reading news from the verified sources which strictly follow publishing regulations, but are blindly regarding news on Social media as the truth. To illustrate further, the recent riots in NYC were caused due to the spread of fake news on Facebook. In conclusion, it is fair to say that the internet and Social media platforms have undoubtedly provided a common ground for loved ones to stay connected. Still, at the same time, it has also given rise to fake relations and fake news. It is therefore imperative that people using these websites do so with a pinch of salt as the cons outweigh the pros to a fair extent.

On the other hand, I believe that the advantages of this scenario are more important. Firstly, such relocation of organizations can reduce the population density in the urban areas. As a result, the influx of workers traveling in rush hours which causes traffic congestion would disappear. Secondly, the movement of companies’ headquarters makes way for the construction of more residential areas, so the citizens would no longer have to live in narrow houses and apartments anymore. Finally, factories carry along with them modem production lines to the suburban areas, hence the rural population might have access to such cutting-edge technological advancements, which have been by no means close to them ever.

Peer influence, colloquially recognized as peer pressure, stands as a pervasive dynamic within the socio-ecological framework, casting its defining imprint upon the behavioral paradigms and life circumstances of juveniles. The present exposition aspires to undertake a rigorous exegesis to proffer perspicuity on whether the liabilities intrinsic to peer influence inordinately eclipse its boons.

The beneficial ramifications that emanate from positive peer pressure are unequivocal. Predominantly, it operates as a galvanizing stimulant of unprecedented magnitude. When adolescents are privy to their peers achieving remarkable milestones across a diversity of domains, such as scholastic prowess or athletic endeavors, an incendiary spark of inspiration is kindled. This competitive impetus, an aspirational cascade of achievement, engenders not only personal flourishing but also orchestrates an elevation of accomplishments hitherto deemed unattainable.

Moreover, the profound compass of peer influence extends to the genesis of quintessential social adeptness. Ongoing interaction with peers imparts a nuanced education in the fine arts of negotiation, effective communication, and the nuances of collective decision-making. These quintessential competencies stand as crucial instruments requisite for navigating the labyrinthine precincts of adulthood, enshrining their indispensability in contexts as diverse as professional environs and intricate relational matrices.

However, to confine our reflection solely within the precincts of advantage is to sidestep the abiding adversities concomitant with peer influence. Negative peer pressure, notably pernicious, frequently catalyzes perilous comportment among juveniles. This coersive undercurrent may compel individuals to partake in deleterious activities, encompassing substance consumption and debauched indulgences, to assimilate with their peer cohort. This ignites multifarious threats, not only to the somatic and psychological well-being of these impressionable adolescents but also to the impending specter of legal censure and social reprobation.

Additionally, the regulatory agency of peer influence, far from being an innocuous agent of camaraderie, possesses the latent potential to occlude individuality and extirpate personal identity. The magnetic allure of group conformity, in its more potent manifestations, potentially incites individuals to disavow their dearly held values and renounce their innate passions in the inexorable quest for conformity. The resultant repercussions include arrested self-actualization and the preclusion of the unbridled exploration of unique talents and idiosyncrasies.

In summation, the variegated tapestry of peer influence, replete with contrasting facets, undeniably wields considerable sway over the comportment and vicissitudes of the adolescent cohort. While the boons intrinsic to positive peer pressure are starkly conspicuous, notably in the realms of motivation and the cultvation of pivotal social dexterity, it is incontrovertible that the attendant liabilities, prominently featuring injurious behaviors and the stifling of individuality, are equally trenchant. Thus, it becomes incumbent upon the burgeoning generation to adroitly calibrate the scales of influence, ensuring that the choices they make are circumspect, fostering a trajectory of personal evolution that is both discerning and positive.

essay.text:
In  contemporary society, young individuals who have been subject to peer pressure may have begun to demonstrate emotional and behavioural changes. While this type of pressure can help teens consolidate their behaviour and their performance in the classroom, I assume that it can also have an adverse bearing on their mental health.

It is undeniable that through regular interaction with constructive examples and perspectives of peers, who are in a similar age group or social status, the primary benefit for young students is the possibility of forming and maintaining frequent academic practices. Those adolescents tend to take others, especially those with whom they have admiration, as role models. Consequently, the presence of positive role models boosts the likelihood of academic and even social achievement among young pupils. For example, observing a peer’s success in a prestigious intellectual competition, such as Road to Mount Olympia - a well-known competition for outstanding students to showcase their intelligence - can motivate other students to study industriously and enhance their performance at school.

Nevertheless, I believe that the adverse effects of peer pressure  on an individual's mental well-being overshadow its benefits. It is worth noting that this tendency can increase stress levels in the young, which in turn can make them feel inadequate or become reticent when expressing their opinions and personal ideas. If a sense of anxiety and depression persists without proper adjustment, this can result in the suicide of many emotionally driven young people, a very undesirable outcome. For example, in 2022, a Vietnamese boy committed suicide by jumping off a tall building as a form of protest against his father’s insistence that he studied for a long period of time at the expense of sleep and entertainment. He was so pressured by his father and peers to perform outstandingly in school as well as gain a respectable university in Hanoi that he made an impulsive decision to end his life.

In conclusion, peer pressure has the potential to be a positive force for reinforcing personal abilities,however,I personally believe that its highly devastating impact on students’ mentality.
